### Subplots with Plotly

Plotly’s R graphing library makes it easy to create interactive, publication-quality graphs.

Plotly also has subplot capabilities. This page documents the usage of the `make_subplots()` function. 

#### Simple Subplot

Figures with subplots are created using the `make_subplots()` function, and traces are added to a given subplot with the `row` and `col` arguments of `add_*()`.

Here is an example of creating a figure that includes two `scatter` traces which are side-by-side since there are 2 columns and 1 row in the subplot layout.

```{r}
library(plotly.core)

fig <- make_subplots(rows = 1, cols = 2) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(1, 2, 3),
    y = c(4, 5, 6),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(line = go_scatter_marker_line(width = 3)),
    row = 1,
    col = 1
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(20, 30, 40),
    y = c(50, 60, 70),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(line = go_scatter_marker_line(width = 3)),
    row = 1,
    col = 2
  ) |>
  update_layout(plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6") |>
  update_xaxes(
    zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
    zerolinewidth = 2,
    gridcolor = "#ffff"
  ) |>
  update_yaxes(
    zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
    zerolinewidth = 2,
    gridcolor = "#ffff"
  ) |>
  update_layout(title = "Side By Side Subplots")

fig
```

#### Stacked Subplots

Here is an example of creating a figure with subplots that are stacked on top of each other since there are 3 rows and 1 column in the subplot layout.

```{r}
library(plotly.core)

fig <- make_subplots(rows = 3, cols = 1) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(3, 4, 5),
    y = c(1000, 1100, 1200),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    row = 1,
    col = 1
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(2, 3, 4),
    y = c(100, 110, 120),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    row = 2,
    col = 1
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(0, 1, 2),
    y = c(10, 11, 12),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    row = 3,
    col = 1
  ) |>
  update_layout(title = "Stacked Subplots") |>
  update_layout(plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6") |>
  update_xaxes(
    zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
    zerolinewidth = 2,
    gridcolor = "#ffff"
  ) |>
  update_yaxes(
    zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
    zerolinewidth = 2,
    gridcolor = "#ffff"
  )

fig
```

#### Multiple Subplots

Here is an example of creating a 2 x 2 subplot grid and populating each subplot with  `scatter` trace.

```{r}
library(plotly.core)

fig <- make_subplots(rows = 2, cols = 2) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(1, 2, 3),
    y = c(4, 5, 6),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(line = go_scatter_marker_line(width = 3)),
    row = 1,
    col = 1
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(20, 30, 40),
    y = c(50, 60, 70),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(line = go_scatter_marker_line(width = 3)),
    row = 1,
    col = 2
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(300, 400, 500),
    y = c(600, 700, 800),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(line = go_scatter_marker_line(width = 3)),
    row = 2,
    col = 1
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(4000, 5000, 6000),
    y = c(7000, 8000, 9000),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(line = go_scatter_marker_line(width = 3)),
    row = 2,
    col = 2
  ) |>
  update_layout(plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6") |>
  update_xaxes(
    zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
    zerolinewidth = 2,
    gridcolor = "#ffff"
  ) |>
  update_yaxes(
    zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
    zerolinewidth = 2,
    gridcolor = "#ffff"
  )

fig
```

#### Multiple Subplots with Titles
The `subplot_titles` argument of `make_subplots()` can be used to position text annotations as titles for each subplot.

Here is an example of adding subplot titles to a 2 x 2 subplot grid of scatter traces.

```{r}
library(plotly.core)

fig <- make_subplots(
  rows = 2,
  cols = 2,
  subplot_titles = c("Plot 1", "Plot 2", "Plot 3", "Plot 4")
) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(1, 2, 3),
    y = c(4, 5, 6),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(line = go_scatter_marker_line(width = 3)),
    row = 1,
    col = 1
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(20, 30, 40),
    y = c(50, 60, 70),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(line = go_scatter_marker_line(width = 3)),
    row = 1,
    col = 2
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(300, 400, 500),
    y = c(600, 700, 800),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(line = go_scatter_marker_line(width = 3)),
    row = 2,
    col = 1
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(4000, 5000, 6000),
    y = c(7000, 8000, 9000),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(line = go_scatter_marker_line(width = 3)),
    row = 2,
    col = 2
  ) |>
  update_layout(title = "Multiple Subplots with Titles") |>
  update_layout(plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6") |>
  update_xaxes(
    zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
    zerolinewidth = 2,
    gridcolor = "#ffff"
  ) |>
  update_yaxes(
    zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
    zerolinewidth = 2,
    gridcolor = "#ffff"
  )

fig
```

#### Subplots with Annotations

```{r}
library(plotly.core)

fig <- make_subplots(rows = 1, cols = 2) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(1, 2, 3),
    y = c(4, 5, 6),
    mode = "markers+text",
    text = c("Text D", "Text E", "Text F"),
    textposition = "bottom center",
    texttemplate = "%{text}",
    row = 1,
    col = 1
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(20, 30, 40),
    y = c(50, 60, 70),
    mode = "markers+text",
    text = c("Text D", "Text E", "Text F"),
    textposition = "bottom center",
    texttemplate = "%{text}",
    row = 1,
    col = 2
  ) |>
  update_layout(title = "Subplots with Annotations") |>
  update_layout(plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6") |>
  update_xaxes(
    zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
    zerolinewidth = 2,
    gridcolor = "#ffff"
  ) |>
  update_yaxes(
    zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
    zerolinewidth = 2,
    gridcolor = "#ffff"
  )

fig
```

#### Customize Subplot Column Widths and Row Heights
The `column_widths` argument of `make_subplots()` can be used to customize the relative widths of the columns in a subplot grid. It should be set to a vector of numbers so that they sum to 1, and used to compute the relative widths of the subplot grid columns. The `row_heights` argument serves the same purpose for controlling the relative heights of rows in the subplot grid.

Here is an example of creating a figure with two scatter traces in side-by-side subplots. The left subplot is set to be wider than the right one.

```{r}
library(plotly.core)

fig <- make_subplots(rows = 1, cols = 2, column_widths = c(0.7, 0.3)) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(1, 2, 3),
    y = c(4, 5, 6),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(line = go_scatter_marker_line(width = 3)),
    row = 1,
    col = 1
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(20, 30, 40),
    y = c(50, 60, 70),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(line = go_scatter_marker_line(width = 3)),
    row = 1,
    col = 2
  ) |>
  update_layout(plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6") |>
  update_xaxes(
    zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
    zerolinewidth = 2,
    gridcolor = "#ffff"
  ) |>
  update_yaxes(
    zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
    zerolinewidth = 2,
    gridcolor = "#ffff"
  )

fig
```

#### Subplots in Dash

[Dash for R](https://dashr.plotly.com) is an open-source framework for building analytical applications, with no Javascript required, and it is tightly integrated with the Plotly graphing library.

Learn about how to install Dash for R at https://dashr.plot.ly/installation.

Everywhere in this page that you see fig, you can display the same figure in a Dash for R application by passing it to the figure argument.


```{r eval=FALSE}
library(dash)
library(dashCoreComponents)
library(dashHtmlComponents)
library(plotly.core)

app <- Dash$new()

app$layout(
  htmlDiv(
    list(
      dccGraph(id = "graph-with-slider"),
      htmlLabel("Subplots Width:"),
      dccSlider(
        id = "slider",
        min = 0,
        max = 1,
        value = 0.5,
        step = 0.01
      )
    )
  )
)
app$callback(
  output(id = "graph-with-slider", property = "figure"),
  params = list(input(id = "slider", property = "value")),
  function(value) {
    fig <- make_subplots(
      rows = 1,
      cols = 2,
      column_widths = c(value, 1 - value)
    ) |>
      add_scatter(
        x = c(1, 2, 3),
        y = c(4, 5, 6),
        mode = "lines+markers",
        marker = go_scatter_marker(line = go_scatter_marker_line(width = 3)),
        row = 1,
        col = 1
      ) |>
      add_scatter(
        x = c(20, 30, 40),
        y = c(50, 60, 70),
        mode = "lines+markers",
        marker = go_scatter_marker(line = go_scatter_marker_line(width = 3)),
        row = 1,
        col = 2
      )
    return(fig)
  }
)
```

After executing this code, give app$run_server() in the console to start the dash.

#### Customizing Subplot Axes
After a figure with subplots is created using the `make_subplots()` function, its axis properties (title, font, range, grid style, etc.) can be customized using the `update_xaxes()` and `update_yaxes()` figure functions.  By default, these functions apply to all of the x axes or y axes in the figure. The `row` and `col` arguments can be used to control which axes are targeted by the update.

Here is an example that creates a figure with a 2 x 2 subplot grid, populates each subplot with a scatter trace, and then updates the x and y axis titles for each subplot individually.

```{r}
library(plotly.core)

# initialize figure with subplots
fig <- make_subplots(
  rows = 2,
  cols = 2,
  subplot_titles = c("Plot 1", "Plot 2", "Plot 3", "Plot 4"),
  horizontal_spacing = 0.1,
  vertical_spacing = 0.15
) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(1, 2, 3),
    y = c(4, 5, 6),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(line = go_scatter_marker_line(width = 3)),
    row = 1,
    col = 1
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(20, 30, 40),
    y = c(50, 60, 70),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(line = go_scatter_marker_line(width = 3)),
    row = 1,
    col = 2
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(300, 400, 500),
    y = c(600, 700, 800),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(line = go_scatter_marker_line(width = 3)),
    row = 2,
    col = 1
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(4000, 5000, 6000),
    y = c(7000, 8000, 9000),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(line = go_scatter_marker_line(width = 3)),
    row = 2,
    col = 2
  ) |>
  update_layout(title = "Customizing Subplot Axes") |>
  update_layout(plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6") |>
  update_xaxes(
    zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
    zerolinewidth = 2,
    gridcolor = "#ffff"
  ) |>
  update_yaxes(
    zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
    zerolinewidth = 2,
    gridcolor = "#ffff"
  )

# update axis properties
fig <- fig |>
  update_xaxes(title = "xaxis1 title", row = 1, col = 1) |>
  update_xaxes(title = "xaxis2 title", range = c(10, 50), row = 1, col = 2) |>
  update_xaxes(title = "xaxis3 title", showgrid = FALSE, row = 2, col = 1) |>
  update_xaxes(title = "xaxis4 title", type = "log", row = 2, col = 2) |>
  update_yaxes(title = "yaxis1 title", row = 1, col = 1) |>
  update_yaxes(title = "yaxis2 title", range = c(40, 80), row = 1, col = 2) |>
  update_yaxes(title = "yaxis3 title", showgrid = FALSE, row = 2, col = 1) |>
  update_yaxes(title = "yaxis4 title", row = 2, col = 2)

fig
```

#### Subplots with Shared X-Axes
The `shared_xaxes` argument of `make_subplots()` can be used to link the x axes of subplots in the resulting figure. The `vertical_spacing` argument is used to control the vertical spacing between rows in the subplot grid.

Here is an example that creates a figure with 3 vertically stacked subplots with linked x axes. A small `vertical_spacing` value is used to reduce the spacing between subplot rows.

```{r}
library(plotly.core)

fig <- make_subplots(
  rows = 3,
  cols = 1,
  shared_xaxes = TRUE,
  vertical_spacing = 0.02
) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(3, 4, 5),
    y = c(1000, 1100, 1200),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    row = 1,
    col = 1
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(2, 3, 4),
    y = c(100, 110, 120),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    row = 2,
    col = 1
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(0, 1, 2),
    y = c(10, 11, 12),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    row = 3,
    col = 1
  ) |>
  update_layout(title = "Stacked Subplots with Shared X-Axes") |>
  update_layout(plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6") |>
  update_xaxes(
    zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
    zerolinewidth = 2,
    gridcolor = "#ffff"
  ) |>
  update_yaxes(
    zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
    zerolinewidth = 2,
    gridcolor = "#ffff"
  )

fig
```

#### Subplots with Shared Y-Axes
The `shared_yaxes` argument can be used to link the y axes of subplots in the resulting figure.

Here is an example that creates a figure with a 2 x 2 subplot grid, where the y axes of each row are linked.


```{r}
library(plotly.core)

fig <- make_subplots(rows = 2, cols = 2, shared_yaxes = TRUE) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(1, 2, 3),
    y = c(2, 3, 4),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    row = 1,
    col = 1
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(20, 30, 40),
    y = c(5, 5, 5),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    row = 1,
    col = 2
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(2, 3, 4),
    y = c(600, 700, 800),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    row = 2,
    col = 1
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(4000, 5000, 6000),
    y = c(7000, 8000, 9000),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    row = 2,
    col = 2
  ) |>
  update_layout(title = "Multiple Subplots with Shared Y-Axes") |>
  update_layout(plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6") |>
  update_xaxes(
    zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
    zerolinewidth = 2,
    gridcolor = "#ffff"
  ) |>
  update_yaxes(
    zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
    zerolinewidth = 2,
    gridcolor = "#ffff"
  )

fig
```

### Subplots with Shared Colorscale

To share colorscale information in multiple subplots, you can use a `coloraxis` (see `go_coloraxis()`).

```{r}
library(plotly.core)

fig <- make_subplots(rows = 1, cols = 2, shared_yaxes = TRUE) |>
  add_bar(
    x = c(1, 2, 3),
    y = c(4, 5, 6),
    marker = go_bar_marker(color = c(4, 5, 6), coloraxis = "coloraxis"),
    row = 1,
    col = 1
  ) |>
  add_bar(
    x = c(1, 2, 3),
    y = c(2, 3, 5),
    marker = go_bar_marker(color = c(2, 3, 5), coloraxis = "coloraxis"),
    row = 1,
    col = 2
  ) |>
  update_layout(
    showlegend = FALSE,
    coloraxis = go_coloraxis(colorscale = "RdBu")
  ) |>
  update_layout(plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6") |>
  update_xaxes(
    zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
    zerolinewidth = 2,
    gridcolor = "#ffff"
  ) |>
  update_yaxes(
    zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
    zerolinewidth = 2,
    gridcolor = "#ffff"
  )

fig
```

#### Custom Sized Subplot with Subplot Titles
The `specs` argument of `make_subplots()` is used to custom size the individual plots in the subplot: a subplot can span several columns (`colspan`) or rows (`rowspan`), and `NULL` marks an empty cell.

Here is an example that creates a 2 by 2 subplot grid containing 3 subplots. 

```{r}
library(plotly.core)

fig <- make_subplots(
  rows = 2,
  cols = 2,
  specs = list(
    list(list(), list()),
    list(list(colspan = 2), NULL)
  ),
  subplot_titles = c("First Subplot", "Second Subplot", "Third Subplot")
) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(1, 2),
    y = c(1, 2),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    row = 1,
    col = 1
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(1, 2),
    y = c(1, 2),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    row = 1,
    col = 2
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(1, 2, 3),
    y = c(2, 1, 2),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    row = 2,
    col = 1
  ) |>
  update_layout(title = "Specs with Subplot Title", showlegend = FALSE) |>
  update_layout(plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6") |>
  update_xaxes(
    zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
    zerolinewidth = 2,
    gridcolor = "#ffff"
  ) |>
  update_yaxes(
    zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
    zerolinewidth = 2,
    gridcolor = "#ffff"
  )

fig
```

#### Multiple Custom Sized Subplots

Here is an example that uses the `rowspan` and `colspan` subplot options to create a custom subplot layout with subplots of mixed sizes. 

```{r}
library(plotly.core)

fig <- make_subplots(
  rows = 5,
  cols = 2,
  specs = list(
    list(list(), list(rowspan = 2)),
    list(list(), NULL),
    list(list(rowspan = 2, colspan = 2), NULL),
    list(NULL, NULL),
    list(list(), list())
  ),
  print_grid = TRUE
) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(1, 2),
    y = c(1, 2),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    name = "(1,1)",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(line = go_scatter_marker_line(width = 3)),
    row = 1,
    col = 1
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(1, 2),
    y = c(1, 2),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    name = "(2,1)",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(line = go_scatter_marker_line(width = 3)),
    row = 2,
    col = 1
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(1, 2),
    y = c(1, 2),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    name = "(1,2)",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(line = go_scatter_marker_line(width = 3)),
    row = 1,
    col = 2
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(1, 2),
    y = c(1, 2),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    name = "(3,1)",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(line = go_scatter_marker_line(width = 3)),
    row = 3,
    col = 1
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(1, 2),
    y = c(1, 2),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    name = "(5,1)",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(line = go_scatter_marker_line(width = 3)),
    row = 5,
    col = 1
  ) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = c(1, 2),
    y = c(1, 2),
    mode = "lines+markers",
    name = "(5,2)",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(line = go_scatter_marker_line(width = 3)),
    row = 5,
    col = 2
  ) |>
  update_layout(plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6") |>
  update_xaxes(
    zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
    zerolinewidth = 2,
    gridcolor = "#ffff"
  ) |>
  update_yaxes(
    zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
    zerolinewidth = 2,
    gridcolor = "#ffff"
  )

fig
```

#### Subplots Types
By default, the `make_subplots()` function assumes that the traces that will be added to all subplots are 2-dimensional cartesian traces (e.g. `scatter`, `bar`, `histogram`, `violin`, etc.). Other subplot types (e.g. `"scene"`, `"polar"`, `"domain"`) are set with the `type` of a cell in `specs`:


 - trace type: A trace type name (e.g. `"bar"`, `"contour"`, `"pie"`, `"scatter"`, etc.) which will be used to determine the appropriate subplot type for that trace.

Here is an example that creates and populates a 2 x 2 subplot grid containing 4 different trace types.

```{r}
library(plotly.core)

data <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/plotly/datasets/master/school_earnings.csv")
density <- density(ggplot2::diamonds$carat)

fig <- make_subplots(
  rows = 2,
  cols = 2,
  horizontal_spacing = 0.1,
  vertical_spacing = 0.1
) |>
  add_bar(y = c(2, 3, 1), row = 1, col = 1) |>
  add_scatter(
    data = data,
    x = ~Women,
    y = ~Men,
    text = ~School,
    mode = "markers",
    marker = go_scatter_marker(
      color = ~Gap,
      colorscale = "Reds",
      showscale = FALSE,
      size = ~Gap,
      opacity = 0.5
    ),
    row = 1,
    col = 2
  ) |>
  add_contour(z = volcano, showscale = FALSE, row = 2, col = 1) |>
  add_scatter(
    x = density$x,
    y = density$y,
    mode = "lines",
    fill = "tozeroy",
    row = 2,
    col = 2
  ) |>
  update_xaxes(showgrid = FALSE, row = 1, col = 2) |>
  update_yaxes(showgrid = FALSE, row = 1, col = 2) |>
  update_xaxes(title = "Carat", row = 2, col = 2) |>
  update_yaxes(title = "Density", row = 2, col = 2) |>
  update_layout(showlegend = FALSE) |>
  update_layout(plot_bgcolor = "#e5ecf6") |>
  update_xaxes(
    zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
    zerolinewidth = 2,
    gridcolor = "#ffff"
  ) |>
  update_yaxes(
    zerolinecolor = "#ffff",
    zerolinewidth = 2,
    gridcolor = "#ffff"
  )

fig
```


#### Reference
All of the axis properties are found in `go_xaxis()` and `go_yaxis()`; see also [Axes](axes.html).


